record.paper_title: Recent Results and Open Problems in Evolutionary Multiobjective Optimization
record.original_question: How can benchmark test problems for multi-objective evolutionary algorithms be designed so that they reflect the actual difficulties of real-world problems, rather than only artificial ZDT, DTLZ, Okabe, or WFG-style test suites?

evidence.quote: loosely related to the actual difficulties that real-world problems have.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider the design of benchmark test problems used to evaluate multi-objective evolutionary algorithms (MOEAs). A multi-objective optimization problem consists of a search space X (typically a subset of R^n), a vector-valued objective function F: X -> R^m with m >= 2 components to be minimized simultaneously, and possibly constraint functions g_i: X -> R. The goal of an MOEA is to approximate the Pareto-optimal set { x in X : there is no y in X with F(y) <= F(x) componentwise and F(y) != F(x) } and its image, the Pareto front in R^m.

Widely used artificial benchmark suites — including the ZDT family (Zitzler–Deb–Thiele), the DTLZ family (Deb–Thiele–Laumanns–Zitzler), the Okabe test problems, and the WFG (Walking Fish Group) suite — provide parametric families of such problems with controllable features (e.g. number of objectives, modality, separability, bias, geometry of the Pareto front). However, these suites are only loosely related to the difficulties encountered in real-world multi-objective problems, which typically involve combinations of: expensive or noisy objective evaluations, mixed discrete–continuous variables, many constraints with small feasible regions, dynamic or uncertain parameters, correlated or conflicting objectives with unknown geometry, and complex variable-to-objective interactions.

Problem. Devise a systematic methodology for constructing benchmark test problems for multi-objective evolutionary algorithms that provably (or quantifiably) reflect the structural difficulties present in real-world multi-objective optimization problems. Specifically:

(a) Identify and formally characterize a set of features (difficulty dimensions) F_1, ..., F_k that real-world multi-objective problems exhibit but that the ZDT, DTLZ, Okabe, and WFG suites fail to capture.

(b) Construct a parametric family { P_θ : θ ∈ Θ } of multi-objective problems such that each feature F_j can be independently tuned by a corresponding component of θ, and such that the resulting Pareto sets and Pareto fronts admit a known or analyzable description.

(c) Provide a quantitative measure of similarity between a benchmark problem P_θ and a given real-world problem R, and prove that for any R in a specified class of real-world problems there exist parameters θ for which P_θ is close to R under this measure.
artifact.status_search_result: The design of realistic MOEA benchmarks remains an active and open research direction. Recent works (e.g. the RE real-world problem suite of Tanabe & Ishibuchi, 2020; benchmark surveys on many-objective and constrained optimization) propose collections of real-world-inspired problems but do not provide a definitive, principled framework that captures the full range of real-world difficulties, and no consensus solution to the question has emerged.

status_evidence.title: An easy-to-use real-world multi-objective optimization problem suite
status_evidence.snippet: Tanabe & Ishibuchi (2020) introduce the RE suite of real-world MOPs, arguing that artificial test suites such as ZDT, DTLZ and WFG do not adequately capture real-world difficulties.
status_evidence.claim: The lack of realistic benchmarks beyond ZDT/DTLZ/WFG is still being addressed by new suites, indicating the question is open.

status_evidence.title: Recent Results and Open Problems in Evolutionary Multiobjective Optimization (zbMATH 7631416)
status_evidence.snippet: Listed among open problems: designing benchmarks that reflect actual difficulties of real-world problems rather than artificial ZDT, DTLZ, Okabe, or WFG suites.
status_evidence.claim: Identified as an explicit open problem in a recent survey of EMO.
